_comment: Every game ./gpb capture and ./gpb profile know about, and everything that differs between
them. Adding a game is adding a block here - no script changes.
This file is COMMITTED, unlike gpb.conf. Nothing in it is a secret or a property of one
machine: it is the shape of a game's network, which is the same for everybody working on
the project and is worth reviewing in a diff when it changes.
Paths are relative to this folder. Two games must never share ANY of the paths below -
once two games' addresses are mixed into one file there is no way to tell them apart again.
GpbGames.ps1 refuses to run while two games declare the same file, and every file is
declared per game rather than falling back to PUBG's name.
FIELDS
name              what the game is called, for messages and a new profile
watchProcess      process to wait for, WITHOUT .exe - Capture-GameTraffic -WatchProcess
probePort         UDP port the game probes datacentres on, to harvest landmarks;
null when the game has no such mechanism, and then no landmark is
collected and landmarkPath stays empty
observedPath      where capture appends the addresses it attributes to the game
landmarkPath      where capture appends probe endpoints; null when probePort is null
tcpSessionsPath   where capture -Protocol tcp writes its diagnosis
unverifiedPath    where the builder lists observed addresses it could not vouch for
manualCidrPath    ranges added by hand that the builder must keep
profilePath       the profile the builder writes; created on the first run if missing
awsRegions        AWS regions whose published EC2 ranges an observed address may belong to
azureRegions      the same for Azure
globalAccelerator true when the game is reached through AWS Global Accelerator. Those
anycast addresses are published only as GLOBAL /17s shared by every GA
customer, so a match is routed as exactly that /32 and never widened
asns              autonomous systems the game owns outright; their BGP-announced prefixes
(RIPEstat) count as published ranges, clamped like a cloud prefix
note              anything a person needs to know before trusting the numbers above
awsRegions, azureRegions, globalAccelerator and asns are the builder's cross-check: an
observed address inside none of them is treated as unverified and kept out of the profile.
A game with none of them declared gets no profile - see the note on cs2. That is not a
default to leave in place; it means the cross-check is missing, and ./gpb profile says so
rather than writing a profile that looks finished.
Whatever is declared, one game's profile never covers an address another game was observed
on: the builder narrows a block until it holds none of them, and Test-Profile.ps1 fails a
profile whose ranges overlap another game's.

pubg.name: PUBG
pubg.note: Gameplay is UDP on Azure and AWS Asia. The game picks its region by probing one endpoint per Azure region on UDP 8081, which is what probePort harvests. The lobby is TCP 40002 on an AWS Global Accelerator and is declared on the licence server, not here.

cs2.name: Counter-Strike 2
cs2.note: ./gpb profile does not build this game, and does not need to: the licence server keeps CS2's ranges equal to Valve's published relay list (web-service/scripts/sync-sdr.ts), and profiles/cs2-vn.json is the self-hosted copy of the same list. The rest of this note is why capture alone could not. CS2 carries gameplay over Steam Datagram Relay: the client talks UDP to a Valve relay PoP, not to the match server, so an observed address belongs to Valve's own network and matches no AWS or Azure range. The cross-check above is therefore empty on purpose and ./gpb profile will refuse rather than write an empty profile. What it needs instead is the PoP list Valve publishes for appid 730, which also removes the need to widen prefixes statistically the way PUBG does. Region ranking has the same problem: there is no UDP 8081 equivalent, so landmarks must come from that PoP list too - until they do, relays are compared on the first leg alone, which the client already handles and logs.

valorant.name: VALORANT
valorant.note: Riot publishes no server list: its peering page (riotgames.com/en/peering-information) gives BGP policy only. What IS public is what the cross-check uses. Vietnamese accounts play on the AP shard, Singapore and Hong Kong. Community captures (github.com/alexonpeace/valorant_servers, Feb 2026) put Singapore on Riot Direct 151.106.248.0/24 - announced by AS6507 - and on AWS Global Accelerator anycast addresses, which ip-ranges.json publishes only as GLOBAL /17s; hence asns and globalAccelerator. Tokyo (ap-northeast-1) is there for players the matchmaker spills over. Unknown until the first capture: whether the game probes regions on a port of its own (probePort stays null until one is seen, so nothing is ever mistaken for a landmark), and whether its latency probe shares the gameplay address the way CS2's does. Read the port column of the first capture before trusting the profile.

lol.name: League of Legends
lol.note: Not captured yet. Riot publishes ports, not servers: the match is UDP 5000-5500 (and 7000-8000) from League of Legends.exe, which only runs during a match - LeagueClient.exe is the lobby and is not watched. Vietnam moved to Riot's own servers in January 2025 (VNG publishes), first hosted in Hong Kong, later on hardware in Vietnam. Whether those servers sit inside AS6507's announcements is unknown - an address outside them lands in observed-lol-unverified.txt, which is the first thing to read after a capture. AS6507 is also VALORANT's, so the two games may share prefixes; the builder's overlap rule decides that, never loosen it.
